```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Package versions are pinned via renv (see renv.lock); run renv::restore() to install.
# Functions are called with explicit pkg:: prefixes rather than attaching via library().

# Headline numbers used in the Summary. The price shock is written by the export-price-shock
# chunk below; the land-use results by r/land_use_model/03_summarise_results.R.
shock_2035 <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv"))
lum <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "land_use_country_results.csv.gz"))

# Soybean oil's share of soybean crush value (Janzen & Wang 2025; see Methods). Must match
# SOY_OIL_VALUE_SHARE in r/land_use_model/01_prepare_data.R.
soy_oil_value_share <- 4.72 / (4.72 + 8.66)

# Roberts & Schlenker (2013), Table 1 (p. 2279): supply and demand elasticities of world caloric
# production in six specifications, instrumental variables (IV) and three-stage least squares (3SLS),
# each with 3, 4 and 5 spline knots. The primary scenario uses the central values, 0.10 and -0.05,
# about the average of the six. Each specification estimates supply and demand together, so the
# sensitivity runs use matched pairs: the specifications with the smallest and largest multiplier,
# not the extremes of each range.
eps_s_rs <- 0.10
eps_d_rs <- -0.05
rs_specs <- data.frame(
  spec = c("IV, 3 knots", "IV, 4 knots", "IV, 5 knots", "3SLS, 3 knots", "3SLS, 4 knots", "3SLS, 5 knots"),
  eps_s = c(0.102, 0.096, 0.087, 0.116, 0.112, 0.097),
  eps_d = c(-0.028, -0.055, -0.054, -0.034, -0.062, -0.066)
)
stopifnot(
  "The central values should be about the average of the six specifications" =
    abs(mean(rs_specs$eps_s) - eps_s_rs) < 0.005 && abs(mean(rs_specs$eps_d) - eps_d_rs) < 0.005
)
# Price multiplier M = 1 / (eps_s - eps_d); eps_d is negative, so the denominator is eps_s + |eps_d|.
multiplier <- function(eps_s, eps_d) 1 / (eps_s - eps_d)
m_rs <- multiplier(eps_s_rs, eps_d_rs) # ~6.7
rs_specs$m <- multiplier(rs_specs$eps_s, rs_specs$eps_d)
rs_low <- rs_specs[which.min(rs_specs$m), ]
rs_high <- rs_specs[which.max(rs_specs$m), ]

# The model runs: the primary shock; the same shock on palm and on soybeans alone, to split the loss
# by crop; and the shocks at the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates.
scenarios <- c("vo_rs", "vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy", "vo_rs_low", "vo_rs_high")

# Additional forest loss relative to BAU: BAU stock minus scenario stock, so positive = more loss.
# lum has one row per country x scenario x year (checked in 03_summarise_results.R).
bau <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "bau") |>
  dplyr::select(country, year, carbon_bau = forest_carbon_tco2, area_bau = forest_area_ha)
loss <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% scenarios) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(bau, by = c("country", "year")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    carbon_loss = carbon_bau - forest_carbon_tco2, # t CO2
    area_loss = area_bau - forest_area_ha # ha
  )
stopifnot(
  "Every run needs every country and year" =
    nrow(loss) == length(scenarios) * nrow(bau) && !anyDuplicated(loss[c("country", "scenario", "year")])
)
global_loss <- loss |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    dplyr::across(c(carbon_loss, area_loss, carbon_bau, area_bau), sum),
    .by = c(scenario, year)
  )
gl <- function(scn, yr, var) global_loss[[var]][global_loss$scenario == scn & global_loss$year == yr]

final_year <- max(lum$year)
n_years <- final_year - min(lum$year)
country_final <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(year == final_year) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = carbon_loss / sum(carbon_loss), .by = scenario) |>
  dplyr::arrange(scenario, dplyr::desc(carbon_loss))
rs_final <- country_final |> dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs")
# Countries whose additional loss peaks and then narrows by >5% (BAU later clears some of the
# same forest), among those with more than 1 Mt CO2 of additional loss.
gap_peaks <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    peak = max(carbon_loss),
    peak_year = year[which.max(carbon_loss)],
    final = carbon_loss[year == final_year],
    .by = country
  )
n_narrowing <- sum(gap_peaks$peak > 1e6 & gap_peaks$final < 0.95 * gap_peaks$peak)
mys <- gap_peaks[gap_peaks$country == "Malaysia", ]

# ILUC carbon intensity: additional forest carbon loss after T years of fuel use, divided by T
# years of VO-RD energy at the 2035 level. Annual VO-RD energy is ICCT's 2035 VO-RD share of
# shipping energy (Table 1), saved by the tbl-icct-table-1 chunk below.
icct_saved <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "icct_table_1.csv"))
icct_2035 <- icct_saved[icct_saved$year == 2035, ]
vord_mj_2035 <- icct_2035$vord_pct_energy_demand / 100 * icct_2035$shipping_energy_demand_ej * 1e12
vord_direct_ci <- 42.3 # g CO2e/MJ, soy VO-RD (Seber & Pavlenko 2025, p. 6)
fossil_baseline_ci <- 93.3 # g CO2e/MJ, 2008 baseline (Seber & Pavlenko 2025, p. 1)
accounting_years <- c(20, 25, 30)
headline_years <- 25
iluc <- expand.grid(
  scenario = c("vo_rs", "vo_rs_low", "vo_rs_high"),
  years = accounting_years,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
iluc$carbon_loss <- mapply(
  function(scn, yrs) gl(scn, min(lum$year) + yrs, "carbon_loss"),
  iluc$scenario, iluc$years
)
iluc$g_per_mj <- iluc$carbon_loss * 1e6 / (iluc$years * vord_mj_2035)
iluc <- iluc[order(iluc$scenario, iluc$years), ]
il <- function(scn, yrs) iluc$g_per_mj[iluc$scenario == scn & iluc$years == yrs]
# Where an ILUC value sits relative to ICCT's 62 and Chen et al.'s 84.1 g CO2e/MJ, for the text.
vs_benchmarks <- function(x) if (x < 62) "below both" else if (x > 84.1) "above both" else "between them"

# Closest benchmark: Chen et al.'s ILUC from forest biomass carbon alone, the only pool we count. They
# study forest-to-palm conversion in Indonesia and Malaysia only, so we also give those countries' part
# of our headline value.
chen_biomass_iluc <- 58.7 # g CO2e/MJ, biomass carbon (AGB + BGB) (Chen et al. 2026, Table 1, p. 13)
iluc_of <- function(countries, scn = "vo_rs", yrs = headline_years) {
  rows <- loss$scenario == scn & loss$year == min(lum$year) + yrs & loss$country %in% countries
  sum(loss$carbon_loss[rows]) * 1e6 / (yrs * vord_mj_2035)
}
im_iluc <- iluc_of(c("Indonesia", "Malaysia"))
drc_iluc <- iluc_of("Democratic Republic of the Congo")

# Crop attribution: palm-only and soy-only runs of the Roberts & Schlenker shock. They sum to the joint run
# to within the interaction term reported here.
crop_split <- c(
  palm = gl("vo_rs_palm", final_year, "carbon_loss"),
  soy = gl("vo_rs_soy", final_year, "carbon_loss")
)
interaction_pct <- 100 * (gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss") - sum(crop_split)) /
  gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss")

fmt1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
fmt0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
# Elasticities at their source's precision, two or three decimals (0.10, −0.028), with a true minus sign.
fmt_el <- function(x) {
  digits <- ifelse(abs(round(x, 2) - x) < 1e-9, 2, 3)
  sub("^-", "−", mapply(formatC, x, format = "f", digits = digits))
}
# Country names as they read mid-sentence ("the Democratic Republic of the Congo").
the_country <- function(x) {
  ifelse(grepl("^(Democratic Republic|Republic of|Central African Republic|United States|United Kingdom|United Republic|Philippines|Netherlands|Gambia|Ivory Coast|Solomon Islands)", x), paste("the", x), x)
}

# Figures: one ggplot2 theme and one set of colors throughout. The primary scenario and crops keep
# the same colors in every figure; magnitude on maps uses viridisLite's magma, reversed so darker
# means more loss (the ends are trimmed so the lightest step stays visible on the gray land).
col_surface <- "#fcfcfb"
col_land <- "#ecebe6"
col_primary <- "#2a78d6"
col_range <- "#9cc3ee" # low-high range of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates
col_crop <- c("Oil palm" = "#1baf7a", "Soybeans" = "#eda100")
map_ramp <- function(n) viridisLite::magma(n, direction = -1, begin = 0.1, end = 0.95)

theme_report <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = col_surface, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
theme_map <- function() {
  theme_report() +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.justification = "center"
    )
}

# Country outlines (Natural Earth 1:110m), as vertices; see r/make_basemap.R.
basemap <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "natural_earth", "ne_110m_admin_0_countries.csv.gz"))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Preliminary and exploratory

This is a prototype, and its numbers are rough. Read them as the likely scale of the effect rather than as estimates for policy, regulation or carbon accounting, and expect them to change as the work develops.

Three things matter most. The price shock that drives everything else comes from a simple formula meant for small changes, while marine demand would equal `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of today's world vegetable-oil production. The elasticities in that formula are Roberts & Schlenker's estimates for staple crops, not vegetable oils. And the country results are the least reliable part: we apply one world price everywhere, and the model's broad crop zones send some of the palm response to Central Africa ([Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix)). We also count only carbon in forest biomass, so peat and soil carbon are missing. The [Caveats](#sec-caveats) section has the full list.
:::

## Summary

ICCT estimates that meeting the Net-Zero Framework's Base target at least cost takes about `r fmt0(shock_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters)` billion liters of virgin vegetable oil a year for marine renewable diesel (VO-RD) by 2035 [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. That is `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of current world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflower oil.

Supply and demand elasticities measure how much production and consumption change when prices rise by 1%. We take both from Roberts & Schlenker's widely used estimates for staple crops: a supply elasticity of `r fmt_el(eps_s_rs)` and a demand elasticity of `r fmt_el(eps_d_rs)` [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279]. With these, marine demand raises vegetable-oil prices by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%. That comes from a linear approximation stretched far beyond its range, so we use it to size the land-use model's inputs, not as a price forecast.

emLab's land-use model, which turns prices into forest loss, prices palm as oil but soybeans as whole beans, and oil is about 35% of a crushed soybean's value [@janzen2025, Fig. 2]. Holding meal prices fixed, the shock raises palm oil prices `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices `r fmt0(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%.

At those prices, the emLab model clears an extra `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha of forest in 15 years compared with business as usual (BAU), releasing `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. Over its full `r n_years`-year run the totals are `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha and `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. The palm price increase causes `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the extra loss. `r sub("^the ", "The ", the_country(rs_final$country[1]))` and `r the_country(rs_final$country[2])` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(rs_final$share[1:2]))`% of it, but the country split is the least reliable part of the analysis.

Spread over `r headline_years` years of fuel use, the extra loss comes to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))` g CO₂ per MJ of VO-RD (`r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 20))` over 20 years, `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 30))` over 30). Adding VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ [@seber2025, p. 6] gives `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))` g/MJ, against a fossil baseline of `r fossil_baseline_ci`. Across Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications, the price shock runs from `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low)`% to `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high)`% and the `r headline_years`-year ILUC value from `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_low", 25))` to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_high", 25))` g CO₂/MJ (@tbl-iluc-sensitivity).

For comparison, ICCT has used an ILUC value of 62 g CO₂e/MJ [@sturrup2026, p. 10], and @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] estimate 84.1 for palm. Our value is `r vs_benchmarks(il("vo_rs", 25))`. Both benchmarks are ILUC alone, like ours, so ICCT's 62 compares with our `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))`, not with our total of `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))`. We count only forest biomass carbon, so the closest benchmark is Chen et al.'s biomass carbon alone, `r chen_biomass_iluc` g CO₂e/MJ; peat added another 47.5 [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13]. Our value is close to it, but only `r fmt1(im_iluc)` g/MJ of ours comes from Indonesia and Malaysia, the two countries they study, and `r fmt1(drc_iluc)` from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The agreement is partly a coincidence.

## Background

### The IMO Net-Zero Framework

In April 2025 the International Maritime Organization approved draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI [@sturrup2026, p. 1] that set greenhouse-gas fuel-intensity (GFI) targets for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above. GFI is well-to-wake g CO₂e/MJ, measured against a 2008 baseline of 93.3 [@seber2025, p. 1]. The Base target tightens from a 4% cut in 2028 to 30% by 2035, and the stricter Direct Compliance target from 17% to 43%. Ships above the Base target pay \$380 per tonne of excess CO₂e (Tier 2), and ships between the two targets pay \$100 (Tier 1) [@seber2025, pp. 1–2].

As of October 2026 the framework has not been adopted. At an extraordinary session in October 2025, a Saudi Arabian motion to adjourn for a year passed with 57 votes, including 15 countries that had backed the framework in April [@carbonbrief2026]. MEPC 84 (27 April–1 May 2026) kept the April 2025 text as the basis for further work, invited alternatives, and scheduled two more meetings of its intersessional working group on greenhouse gases [@carbonbrief2026; @abs2026mepc84, p. 4]. The first, ISWG-GHG 22 (1–4 September 2026), ended without agreement [@shipandbunker2026]. The sharpest split is over the GHG price and the central IMO fund it pays into. By one observer's count of the countries that spoke, 38 supported them and 17, mostly oil producers, opposed them, and the United States again rejected any IMO-run fund [@shipandbunker2026]. The early GFI trajectory and the rules for pooling compliance surpluses are also unresolved [@maritimeexecutive2026]. Japan's proposal to replace the fund with direct payments from shipowners won little support in September [@maritimeexecutive2026]; its revised version drops the fund and has ships cover shortfalls by buying surplus units from other ships [@marineinsight2026].

The working group meets again 23–27 November, followed by MEPC 85 (30 November–3 December). If MEPC 85 agrees, the extraordinary session resumes on 4 December 2026 and could vote that day [@abs2026mepc84, p. 4; @shipandbunker2026]. Whatever is adopted may differ from the April 2025 text we start from: a gentler early trajectory would mean less biofuel demand, and dropping the GHG price would change the compliance costs that set the fuel mix.

The framework judges fuels on their direct life-cycle emissions only. The IMO's life-cycle guidelines treat ILUC as too uncertain to give each fuel a number, and handle it through a qualitative, risk-based approach instead [@imo2024lca, paras. 4.12–4.13]. MEPC 84 supported this in principle and asked for more quantitative analysis by MEPC 85 [@abs2026mepc84, p. 6]. Because blending biofuel costs less than the \$380 Tier 2 penalty, the cheapest strategy is to blend just enough to meet the Base target. In ICCT's least-cost mix, used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) runs out at about 5% of shipping energy and virgin vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) covers the rest, reaching 46% of shipping energy by 2035 [@seber2025, p. 4 and Table 1, p. 5].

ICCT's Table 1 gives the mix for each year from 2028 to 2035. We read it straight from the PDF; its last column, virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, is our demand shift.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icct-table-1

pdf_path <- file.path(
  "data",
  "icct_biofuel_demand_report",
  "ID-450-Vegetable-Oil_research-brief_final.pdf"
)

# Extract page 5 as text and keep only the data rows (years 2028–2035)
page5 <- pdftools::pdf_text(pdf_path)[5]
lines <- stringr::str_trim(stringr::str_split(page5, "\n")[[1]])
data_lines <- stringr::str_subset(lines, "^20(2[89]|3[0-5])\\b")

# Each data row yields exactly 10 numeric tokens:
#   year, shipping demand, base target, fossil LNG %,
#   UCO-RD %, UCO-RD bl, VO-RD %, VO-RD bl, UCO demand bl, VO demand bl
nums <- stringr::str_extract_all(data_lines, "[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*")
mat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(nums, function(x) as.numeric(x[seq_len(10)])))

icct_table_1 <- tibble::as_tibble(mat, .name_repair = "minimal")
names(icct_table_1) <- c(
  "year",
  "shipping_energy_demand_ej",
  "base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj",
  "fossil_lng_pct",
  "ucord_pct_energy_demand",
  "ucord_billion_liters",
  "vord_pct_energy_demand",
  "vord_billion_liters",
  "uco_demand_billion_liters",
  "vo_demand_billion_liters"
)

icct_table_1 <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

# Saved for the setup chunk, which needs the 2035 VO-RD energy for the ILUC calculation.
utils::write.csv(icct_table_1, file.path("data", "derived", "icct_table_1.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(
  icct_table_1 |>
    dplyr::select(
      year,
      shipping_energy_demand_ej,
      base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj,
      ucord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_billion_liters,
      vo_demand_billion_liters
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "Shipping energy (EJ)",
    "Base target (g CO₂e/MJ)",
    "UCO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD fuel (billion L)",
    "Virgin VO feedstock (billion L)"
  ),
  caption = "ICCT Table 1, selected columns [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, the last column, is the demand shock D."
)
```

The direct carbon intensities behind the mix:

| Fuel | Life-cycle carbon intensity (g CO₂e/MJ) |
|---|---|
| 2008 baseline | 93.3 |
| Heavy fuel oil (HFO) | 92.8 |
| Fossil LNG | 85.7 |
| Soy vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) | 42.3 |
| Soy FAME biodiesel | 35.7 |
| Used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) | 13.1 |

: Direct life-cycle carbon intensities used by ICCT: 2008 baseline (p. 1); fossil LNG, 85.65 (p. 2); HFO, 92.78, soy VO-RD, soy FAME (35.74) and UCO-RD (p. 6) [@seber2025]. None include indirect land-use change. {#tbl-direct-ci}

### Indirect land-use change

Indirect land-use change (ILUC) happens when biofuel demand raises crop prices and the higher prices lead to forest being cleared for farmland elsewhere. Those emissions fall outside the fuel's own supply chain, so a fuel mix can meet the GFI targets on paper while adding emissions nobody counts. @fig-steps shows our steps.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-steps
%%| fig-cap: "From the IMO Net-Zero Framework to an ILUC carbon intensity: the steps, and who supplies each."
flowchart LR
  A["IMO Net-Zero Framework"] --> F["Marine VO-RD demand<br/><i>ICCT cost-optimization</i>"]
  F --> B["Virgin vegetable-oil demand<br/><i>1.22 kg oil per kg RD</i>"]
  B --> C["Vegetable-oil price shock<br/><i>this report</i>"]
  C --> D["Forest loss by country<br/><i>emLab land-use model</i>"]
  D --> E["ILUC carbon intensity<br/><i>this report</i>"]
```

ICCT converts renewable diesel to oil at 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel [@seber2025, p. 3, note 9].

Published ILUC estimates for vegetable-oil biofuels vary widely (@tbl-published-iluc).

| Source | Approach | ILUC result |
|---|---|---|
| ICCT climate & revenue brief [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11] | Fixed factor applied to ICCT's demand projection | 62 g CO₂e/MJ; ~285 Mt CO₂e/yr by 2035; ~950 Mt CO₂e over 2028–2035 |
| U.S. EPA model comparison [@epa2023mce, Table 7.7-1, p. 113] | Five models, soybean-oil biodiesel shock | Land-use change: 10 to 295 kg CO₂e/MMBTU (GCAM: 62) |
| @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] | Econometric estimates of demand → price → deforestation for palm, 2002–2018 | 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ (90% CI 48.7–113.5) |
| GLOBIOM for the EU [@valin2015, p. x] | Global economic land-use model, emissions spread over 20 years | 231 g CO₂e/MJ for palm oil, 150 for soybean oil |

: ICCT takes its 62 from the EPA model comparison [@sturrup2026, p. 10]. The only 62 in the EPA's results table is GCAM's land-use-change value, in kg CO₂e/MMBTU (≈ 59 g CO₂e/MJ), so we assume that is the source. Every value here is ILUC alone, without the fuel's direct emissions. ICCT adds its 62, weighted by VO-RD's share of shipping energy (62 × 46% ≈ 28.5 g CO₂e/MJ in 2035), to the fleet's Base-target GFI [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11], which puts the ILUC-adjusted fleet GFI at 93.86 g CO₂e/MJ in 2035, above the fossil baseline [@sturrup2026, Table A1, p. 15]. {#tbl-published-iluc}

Like Chen et al., we estimate how much the demand shift raises prices and then use an econometric land-use model to turn prices into forest loss, rather than assume an ILUC factor.

## Methods and assumptions

The analysis has five steps:

1. Turn ICCT's 2035 vegetable-oil demand into a price shock, with Roberts & Schlenker's central supply and demand elasticities.
2. Translate the shock into prices for the emLab model's crops.
3. Run the model with baseline and shocked prices, both at a zero carbon price, and take the difference in forest loss.
4. Spread the extra emissions over the fuel used, to get g CO₂ per MJ.
5. Repeat steps 1–4 at the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates, for a range.

### From demand to a price shock {#sec-price-shock}

When demand shifts out, the price rises by roughly the size of the shift divided by the gap between the supply and demand elasticities [@roberts2013, Table 1, panel C, p. 2279]:

$$ \%\Delta P \;\approx\; \underbrace{\frac{D}{Q_0}}_{\text{demand shift}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_s - \varepsilon_d}}_{\text{multiplier } M} $$

where $D$ is marine virgin vegetable-oil demand and $Q_0$ is baseline world production. The supply elasticity $\varepsilon_s > 0$ is the percentage rise in production when prices rise 1%, and the demand elasticity $\varepsilon_d < 0$ is the percentage change in consumption. The multiplier $M$ is the percentage price rise for each percentage point of demand shift: the less supply and demand respond, the larger it is.

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Marine virgin vegetable-oil demand, 2035 ($D$) | 139.3 billion L | ICCT [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5] |
| Baseline market ($Q_0$) | ≈ 204 Mt: world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflowerseed oil, 2024/25 | USDA Production, Supply and Distribution (PSD) database [@usdapsd] |
| Oil density, to put $D$ and $Q_0$ in the same units | 0.92 kg/L | ICCT's own soy-oil conversion: 12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L (0.919 kg/L) [@seber2025, Table A1, p. 7] |
| Supply elasticity ($\varepsilon_s$) | `r fmt_el(eps_s_rs)` (low end `r fmt_el(rs_low$eps_s)`, high end `r fmt_el(rs_high$eps_s)`) | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279]: about the average of their six specifications, which range from `r fmt_el(min(rs_specs$eps_s))` to `r fmt_el(max(rs_specs$eps_s))` |
| Demand elasticity ($\varepsilon_d$) | `r fmt_el(eps_d_rs)` (low end `r fmt_el(rs_low$eps_d)`, high end `r fmt_el(rs_high$eps_d)`) | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279]: about the average of their six specifications, which range from `r fmt_el(max(rs_specs$eps_d))` to `r fmt_el(min(rs_specs$eps_d))` |
| Demand year | 2035 only | Our choice: the final year of the ICCT projection |
| "Beyond marginal" flag | demand share > 25% | Our own cutoff for where the approximation gets unreliable (not from a source) |

: Inputs to the price shock. The central multiplier is $M \approx$ `r fmt1(m_rs)`; the low and high ends use `r fmt1(rs_low$m)` and `r fmt1(rs_high$m)`. {#tbl-price-shock-inputs}

$Q_0$ is world production of the four oils in 2024/25, summed across countries from USDA's PSD oilseeds data, downloaded on 31 July 2026 [@usdapsd]. USDA revises PSD continuously, so a later download may differ slightly.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q0

psd_zip_path <- file.path("data", "usda_psd_oilseeds", "psd_oilseeds_csv.zip")
psd <- utils::read.csv(unz(psd_zip_path, "psd_oilseeds.csv"))

q0_market_year <- 2024 # marketing year 2024/25

psd_four_oils <- psd |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Commodity_Description %in%
      c("Oil, Palm", "Oil, Soybean", "Oil, Rapeseed", "Oil, Sunflowerseed"),
    Attribute_Description == "Production",
    Market_Year == q0_market_year
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    production_mt = sum(Value) / 1000, # reported in 1000 MT
    .by = Commodity_Description
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(production_mt))
q0_mt <- sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt) # ~204 Mt

knitr::kable(
  psd_four_oils,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Commodity", "World production, 2024/25 (million t)"),
  caption = paste0(
    "World production of the four major vegetable oils (USDA PSD). Total: ",
    round(sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt), 1),
    " million t."
  )
)
```

Notes on these choices:

- Vegetable oils substitute for one another, so we treat them as one market even though ships would burn soy oil [@chen2026, p. 4]. Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities describe the world market for calories from maize, wheat, rice and soybeans; we use them as a stand-in for vegetable oils.
- Roberts & Schlenker estimate supply and demand together in six specifications: instrumental variables (IV) and three-stage least squares (3SLS), each with 3, 4 or 5 spline knots [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279]. For the range, we rerun everything with the two specifications that give the smallest and largest multiplier, keeping each one's supply and demand elasticities together rather than pairing the extremes of each range (@tbl-price-shock-check).
- We keep the supply elasticity in the multiplier because the emLab model takes prices as given, so the price we give it should already reflect the supply response. Dropping it would give $M = 20$ and triple the shock.
- The formula is a linear approximation, and marine demand is a large share of the market from about 2032, so the 2035 shock gives the scale of the effect, not its size. Roberts & Schlenker also note that, allowing for uncertainty in the elasticities, the expected multiplier is higher than the one from their central estimates [@roberts2013, p. 2280].
- Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity is the output response to the price expected at planting, a year ahead. They argue it is not just a short-run lower bound, because farmers expect price changes to persist [@roberts2013, p. 2285]. Oil palm, by contrast, takes about four years to start fruiting [@chen2026, p. 4].
- Crushing soybeans also yields meal, whose revenue relieves some of the pressure on oil prices. Roberts & Schlenker cut their price effect by a third when a third of the calories return as animal feed [@roberts2013, p. 2280]. We make no such adjustment, so on this count our shock is too high.
- With Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities, the formula reproduces their headline price effect (@tbl-price-shock-check).

### Mapping the shock to the model's crops {#sec-mapping}

Following @chen2026 [p. 3], we apply the same percentage shock to all vegetable-oil prices. Palm oil prices respond to production shocks in competing oil crops about as strongly as to shocks in palm itself (their Fig. 2A, p. 4), and the four oil prices move together in the long run, almost one-for-one [cointegrating coefficients of 1.04 for soybean, 1.01 for canola and 0.86 for sunflower oil, @chen2026, Table S5]. Other work adds nuance: @cui2017 [abstract] find that soy oil diverted to US biodiesel is replaced mostly by palm oil, and @santeramo2017 [p. 13] finds a mix of substitutes and complements that varies by oil and region. Letting each oil's price respond differently would be a sensible refinement.

Only two of the model's 17 crops produce vegetable oil: palm, priced per tonne of palm oil, and soybeans, priced per tonne of beans. According to the emLab model's code, their baseline prices are observed 2020 prices: \$768/t for palm and \$415/t for soybeans, both within 2% of the World Bank's 2020 averages (\$752/t and \$407/t). Soybean oil averaged \$838/t that year [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1].

| Model crop | Shock | Why | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palm oil | $\%\Delta P$ | The model prices palm as oil | — |
| Soybeans | $s \times \%\Delta P$, with $s = 0.353$ | Oil is only part of a soybean's value, and we hold the meal price fixed. $s = \$4.72 / (\$4.72 + \$8.66)$, from the 2007–2025 average per-bushel values of soybean oil and meal | @janzen2025 [Fig. 2] (USDA AMS Illinois plant prices; 11 lb oil and 48 lb meal per bushel) |
| Rapeseed/canola, sunflower | not modeled | Not among the model's crops | — |

: How the oil-price shock enters the emLab model. {#tbl-crop-mapping}

Two checks on $s$: Irwin's 2007–2017 averages (\$4.43 oil, \$8.33 meal) give 0.347 [@irwin2017, Fig. 3], and World Bank 2020 prices (\$838/t oil, \$394/t meal) give 0.33 [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1]. The share swings week to week: between 25% and 35% over 2013–2020, rarely below 35% since, and briefly 50% in 2021 and 2025 [@janzen2025, Fig. 3]. It is an accounting share, not an estimate of how soybean prices respond.

Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the model, so their land-use response is missing and ILUC is understated. We still define $Q_0$ over all four oils, because they compete in one market; using palm and soy alone would inflate the demand share. In 2024/25, 86% of world rapeseed came from Canada, the EU, China, India, Australia and Russia, and 90% of sunflowerseed from Russia, Ukraine, the EU, Argentina, Kazakhstan and China [@usdapsd], so most of the missing response is probably outside tropical forests. We have not quantified it.

### The emLab land-use model {#sec-land-use-model}

We use emLab's global deforestation model; [Appendix A](#sec-lum-changes) lists every change we made to its code.

It is a statistical model of the share of each grid cell's forest cleared each year, as a function of the cell's potential farm revenue and its remaining tree cover, estimated on 2001–2020 data (29.1 million cell-years). It controls for each cell's fixed characteristics and for conditions in each country and year (technically, a fractional logit with cell and country-by-year fixed effects). A cell's revenue is crop price minus transport cost, times attainable yield, averaged over the 17 crops by their share of harvested area and converted to a present value at a 5% discount rate. Transport cost scales with travel time to port and the crude-oil price.

From 2020 tree cover, the model steps forward a year at a time to 2171 over 1,450,769 grid cells (1/12°, about 9 km across) in 154 countries. Country effects are held at their 2016–2020 average, and cleared forest never grows back.

All runs use a zero carbon price, and BAU uses 2020 prices. The primary run raises palm oil prices by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices by `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%. Two more runs apply that shock to palm and to soybeans separately, to split the loss by crop. Two more repeat the primary run with the price shocks at the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates (`r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low)`% and `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high)`% for palm; [Results](#sec-results-price)). Prices jump once, in the first model year, and stay there, so model year 2035 means 15 years after the shock, not the calendar year.

Forest carbon (t CO₂) is tree cover times carbon density, and forest area (ha) is carbon divided by density, using the model's own conversion. We count lost forest carbon as emissions, which leaves out peat, soil carbon and lost future sequestration. As a sanity check, the model has `r fmt0(sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 1e6)` Mha of forest in 2020, `r fmt0(100 * sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 4.06e9)`% of FAO's 4.06 billion ha [@fao2020fra, p. 1]; the two define forest differently.

We use the model's input data unmodified, and summarize its results by country and by 0.5° grid square; [Appendix A](#sec-lum-changes) gives the file details. Map outlines are Natural Earth's 1:110m countries [@naturalearth].

### ILUC carbon intensity {#sec-iluc-method}

We spread the extra emissions over an accounting period of $T$ years of fuel use:

$$ \text{ILUC}_T = \frac{\Delta C(T)}{T \times E} $$

where $\Delta C(T)$ is the cumulative extra forest carbon loss $T$ years after the shock, and $E$ is one year of VO-RD energy at the 2035 level: ICCT's 46.0% VO-RD share of 10.0 EJ of shipping energy, or 4.60 EJ [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Working forward from the feedstock instead (139.3 billion L of oil at 0.92 kg/L, 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel and 43,980 MJ per tonne of fuel) gives 4.62 EJ [@seber2025, pp. 3 and 6, Table A1]. Because the model applies the 2035 demand level from its first year, $T$ years means $T$ years of fuel use at that level, not a span of calendar years.

There is no standard $T$. The EU uses 20 years [@valin2015, p. 3] and the US EPA 30 [@chen2026, p. 13]. We report 20, 25 and 30 and headline 25, the period Chen et al. use to match the oil palm replanting cycle [@chen2026, p. 13], so our number compares directly with their 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ. ICCT's 62 g CO₂e/MJ comes from the EPA's model comparison, which divides cumulative 2020–2050 emissions by cumulative fuel use over the same years [@epa2023mce, pp. 83–84], so it is closest to our 30-year value.

The result counts only CO₂ from forest biomass. We split it by country using each country's share of the extra loss, and by crop using the palm-only and soy-only runs.

## Results

### Vegetable-oil price shock {#sec-results-price}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-price-shock-check

# Q0 (tbl-q0 chunk) in billion liters at 0.92 kg/L, ICCT's own soy-oil conversion
# (12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L, ICCT Table A1).
oil_density_kg_l <- 0.92
q0_billion_liters <- q0_mt / oil_density_kg_l # ~221 billion L

# %ΔP_t = (D_t / Q0) * M, as a percent, with the central multiplier and at the low and high ends.
# beyond_marginal flags years where the shift exceeds 25% of the market, outside the regime where
# the approximation is reliable.
price_shock <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    vo_demand_billion_liters,
    demand_share_pct = 100 * vo_demand_billion_liters / q0_billion_liters,
    pct_delta_p_rs = demand_share_pct * m_rs,
    pct_delta_p_rs_low = demand_share_pct * rs_low$m,
    pct_delta_p_rs_high = demand_share_pct * rs_high$m,
    beyond_marginal = demand_share_pct > 25
  )
share_2035 <- price_shock$demand_share_pct[price_shock$year == 2035]

# Check: Roberts & Schlenker's ethanol mandate used about 5% of world calories (p. 2277), which they
# estimate raised prices about 30% (p. 2280). The formula should recover that from their elasticities.
ethanol_shift_pct <- 5
rs_table <- rbind(
  data.frame(spec = "Central values (primary scenario)", eps_s = eps_s_rs, eps_d = eps_d_rs, m = m_rs),
  rs_specs
)
rs_table$spec <- ifelse(
  rs_table$spec == rs_low$spec, paste(rs_table$spec, "(low end)"),
  ifelse(rs_table$spec == rs_high$spec, paste(rs_table$spec, "(high end)"), rs_table$spec)
)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Specification" = rs_table$spec,
    "Supply elasticity" = fmt_el(rs_table$eps_s),
    "Demand elasticity" = fmt_el(rs_table$eps_d),
    "Multiplier M" = formatC(rs_table$m, format = "f", digits = 2),
    "Ethanol mandate: %ΔP from a 5% shift" = paste0(fmt0(ethanol_shift_pct * rs_table$m), "%"),
    "Marine demand: %ΔP in 2035" = paste0(fmt0(share_2035 * rs_table$m), "%"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lrrrrr",
  caption = paste(
    "Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279] and the central values we",
    "use, about their average. The ethanol column checks the formula: their ethanol mandate used about 5%",
    "of world calories [@roberts2013, p. 2277], which they estimate raised prices about 30%",
    "[@roberts2013, p. 2280]. The low and high ends, the specifications with the smallest and largest",
    "multiplier, are our sensitivity runs."
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-price-shock

knitr::kable(
  price_shock |>
    dplyr::mutate(beyond_marginal = ifelse(beyond_marginal, "yes", "")),
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "VO demand (billion L)",
    "Share of market (%)",
    "%ΔP, central",
    "%ΔP, low end",
    "%ΔP, high end",
    "Beyond marginal"
  ),
  caption = paste(
    "Vegetable-oil price shock from marine biofuel demand, with Roberts & Schlenker's central elasticities",
    "and at the low and high ends of their estimates. Years marked 'beyond marginal' are outside the range",
    "where the linear approximation holds up."
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-shock
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "The price shock implied by each year's marine vegetable-oil demand, with Roberts & Schlenker's central elasticities (line) and between the low and high ends of their estimates (band). The land-use runs use the 2035 values."

ggplot2::ggplot(price_shock, ggplot2::aes(year, pct_delta_p_rs)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = pct_delta_p_rs_low, ymax = pct_delta_p_rs_high), fill = col_range, alpha = 0.6) +
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-market-2035
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Roberts & Schlenker's demand curve before and after 2035 marine demand, with their supply curve, using their central elasticities. The points mark today's market and the price shock run through the model."

# The vegetable-oil market in 2035: demand before and after ICCT's marine demand D, against supply.
# All curves use the price-shock formula's linear approximation, %dQ = eps x %dP.
shock_rs <- price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs[price_shock$year == 2035]
d_mt <- price_shock$vo_demand_billion_liters[price_shock$year == 2035] * oil_density_kg_l
extra_supply_mt <- eps_s_rs * shock_rs / 100 * q0_mt

curve_names <- c(
  paste0("Demand today (ε = ", fmt_el(eps_d_rs), ")"),
  "Demand with 2035 marine demand",
  paste0("Supply (ε = ", fmt_el(eps_s_rs), ")")
)
p_grid <- seq(-50, 600, by = 10)
market_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[1], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100)),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[2], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100) + d_mt),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[3], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_s_rs * p_grid / 100))
)
market_curves$curve <- factor(market_curves$curve, levels = curve_names)
equilibria <- data.frame(
  q = q0_mt + c(0, extra_supply_mt),
  p = c(0, shock_rs),
  label = c("Today", paste0("+", fmt0(shock_rs), "%"))
)

ggplot2::ggplot(market_curves, ggplot2::aes(q, p, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, p), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "#0b0b0b", colour = col_surface, stroke = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, p, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = -0.3, size = 3.4, colour = "#0b0b0b"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = stats::setNames(c("#8f8d86", "#0b0b0b", col_primary), curve_names),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = stats::setNames(c("22", "solid", "solid"), curve_names), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(150, 350, 50)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(130, 360), ylim = c(-50, 600), expand = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "The world vegetable-oil market in 2035",
    x = "Vegetable oil (Mt a year)",
    y = "Change in vegetable-oil price"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

@fig-market-2035 shows the 2035 market: Roberts & Schlenker's demand curve before and after ICCT's `r fmt0(d_mt)` Mt of marine demand, and their supply curve. Prices rise until extra supply and lower use by other buyers together cover the ships' demand. That takes a rise of `r fmt0(shock_rs)`%, which adds `r fmt0(extra_supply_mt)` Mt a year of supply and cuts other buyers' use by `r fmt0(d_mt - extra_supply_mt)` Mt. This is not a forecast: the shift is far outside the linear formula's range, and with elasticities this small the answer depends mostly on the shape assumed for the curves. Across Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications, the multiplier runs from `r fmt1(rs_low$m)` to `r fmt1(rs_high$m)`, which puts the shock between `r fmt0(share_2035 * rs_low$m)`% and `r fmt0(share_2035 * rs_high$m)`% (@tbl-price-shock-check).

The land-use runs use the 2035 values.

```{r}
#| label: export-price-shock

# Hand-off to the land-use model (full precision, no rounding). 01_prepare_data.R reads
# vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv: the central shock and the low and high ends of Roberts &
# Schlenker's estimates. The central elasticities are saved alongside.
handoff_2035 <- price_shock |>
  dplyr::filter(year == 2035) |>
  dplyr::mutate(eps_s = eps_s_rs, eps_d = eps_d_rs)

dir.create(file.path("data", "derived"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
utils::write.csv(
  handoff_2035,
  file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
utils::write.csv(
  price_shock,
  file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

# The setup chunk read this file for the text above, before this render rewrote it. If it was out
# of date, that text used old numbers: stop so the report is rendered again.
if (!isTRUE(all.equal(shock_2035, as.data.frame(handoff_2035), check.attributes = FALSE))) {
  stop("vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv was out of date and has been rewritten. Render again.")
}

cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    "2035: VO demand %.0f billion L on a Q0 of %.0f billion L (demand share %.0f%%).\n",
    "Roberts & Schlenker: multiplier %.2f, price shock +%.0f%% (low end +%.0f%%, high end +%.0f%%)."
  ),
  handoff_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters,
  q0_billion_liters,
  handoff_2035$demand_share_pct,
  m_rs,
  handoff_2035$pct_delta_p_rs,
  handoff_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low,
  handoff_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high
))
```

### Forest loss {#sec-results-forest}

Extra loss is the difference in forest between the BAU run and the shocked run. It is cumulative, so the last model year gives the total over the whole simulation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forest-loss-global

horizons <- c(2035, 2050, final_year)
global_table <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs", year %in% horizons) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Years after shock" = global_table$year - min(lum$year),
    "Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_loss / 1e9,
    "Mha" = global_table$area_loss / 1e6,
    "% of BAU forest carbon" = 100 * global_table$carbon_loss / global_table$carbon_bau,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Cumulative additional forest loss relative to BAU in the primary scenario, all countries."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-loss-timeseries
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative additional forest carbon loss relative to BAU in the primary scenario, over the full run."

global_ts <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs") |>
  dplyr::mutate(years_after_shock = year - min(lum$year), carbon_gt = carbon_loss / 1e9)

ggplot2::ggplot(global_ts, ggplot2::aes(years_after_shock, carbon_gt)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = col_primary, linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, 25), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Cumulative additional forest carbon loss relative to BAU",
    x = "Years after the price shock",
    y = expression("Gt CO"[2])
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

About half of the full-run loss, `r fmt0(100 * gl("vo_rs", 2035, "carbon_loss") / gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss"))`%, happens in the first 15 years.

#### By country and crop

To split the loss by crop, we ran the primary shock on palm alone and on soybeans alone. Palm accounts for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the extra loss and soybeans for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["soy"]] / sum(crop_split))`%. The two runs add up to the combined run to within `r formatC(abs(interaction_pct), format = "f", digits = 2)`%, so the interaction between them is negligible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-loss-by-crop
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative additional forest carbon loss over the full horizon in the primary scenario, by country, split between the palm-only and soy-only runs."

top_n <- 12
top_countries <- rs_final$country[seq_len(top_n)]
other_label <- sprintf("Other %d countries", sum(rs_final$carbon_loss > 0) - top_n)

crop_by_country <- country_final |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = ifelse(country %in% top_countries, country, other_label),
    crop = ifelse(scenario == "vo_rs_palm", "Oil palm", "Soybeans")
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(carbon_loss) / 1e6, .by = c(label, crop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(c(top_countries, other_label))))
bar_totals <- crop_by_country |> dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(mt), .by = label)

ggplot2::ggplot(crop_by_country, ggplot2::aes(mt, label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(
    ggplot2::aes(fill = crop),
    position = ggplot2::position_stack(reverse = TRUE), # palm first, from zero
    width = 0.62, colour = col_surface, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = bar_totals, ggplot2::aes(label = fmt0(mt)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_crop, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Additional forest carbon loss by country and crop",
    subtitle = "Primary scenario, full horizon",
    x = expression("Mt CO"[2]),
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forest-loss-country
#| tbl-cap: "Cumulative additional forest loss relative to BAU in the primary scenario over the full horizon, by country. Palm and soybean columns are the single-crop runs."

country_table <- country_final |>
  dplyr::filter(carbon_loss > 0) |>
  dplyr::select(country, scenario, carbon_loss, area_loss, area_bau, share)
by_scenario <- function(scn, ...) {
  country_table |> dplyr::filter(scenario == scn) |> dplyr::select(country, ...)
}
country_table <- by_scenario("vo_rs", carbon_loss, area_loss, area_bau, share) |>
  dplyr::left_join(by_scenario("vo_rs_palm", carbon_palm = carbon_loss), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(by_scenario("vo_rs_soy", carbon_soy = carbon_loss), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    country,
    carbon_mt = carbon_loss / 1e6,
    palm_mt = dplyr::coalesce(carbon_palm, 0) / 1e6,
    soy_mt = dplyr::coalesce(carbon_soy, 0) / 1e6,
    area_kha = area_loss / 1e3,
    share_pct = 100 * share,
    pct_of_bau_area = 100 * area_loss / area_bau
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(carbon_mt))

DT::datatable(
  country_table,
  rownames = FALSE,
  colnames = c(
    "Country",
    "Mt CO₂",
    "of which palm",
    "of which soybeans",
    "Thousand ha",
    "Share of total (%)",
    "% of country's BAU forest"
  ),
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
) |>
  DT::formatRound(c("carbon_mt", "palm_mt", "soy_mt", "area_kha", "share_pct", "pct_of_bau_area"), digits = 1)
```

`r sum(rs_final$carbon_loss > 0)` countries lose some extra forest, but `r the_country(rs_final$country[1])`, `r the_country(rs_final$country[2])` and `r the_country(rs_final$country[3])` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(rs_final$share[1:3]))`% of it. Only cells that grow oil palm or soybeans respond, since those are the only prices that change.

Because cleared forest never grows back, BAU can later clear forest that a shocked run cleared earlier. In Malaysia the extra loss peaks at `r fmt0(mys$peak / 1e6)` Mt CO₂ in model year `r mys$peak_year` and falls to `r fmt0(mys$final / 1e6)` Mt CO₂ by `r final_year`, and `r n_narrowing` countries end more than 5% below their peak. Globally the extra loss is still rising at the end of the run. The ILUC estimates only count loss within the accounting period, so this late catch-up doesn't affect them.

```{r}
#| label: area-numbers
#| include: false

# Numbers for the text: how area and carbon rank the countries, and carbon per hectare among the ten
# countries with the most additional area cleared.
carbon_rank <- stats::setNames(seq_len(nrow(rs_final)), rs_final$country)
top10_area <- area_final[seq_len(10), ]
lowest_density <- top10_area[which.min(top10_area$t_per_ha), ]
highest_density <- top10_area[which.max(top10_area$t_per_ha), ]
# Countries among the top_n by area that rank at least three places higher by area than by carbon.
rank_up <- area_final$country[seq_len(top_n)][
  seq_len(top_n) + 3 <= carbon_rank[area_final$country[seq_len(top_n)]]
]
rank_up_text <- if (length(rank_up) > 0) {
  paste0(
    " By area, ", knitr::combine_words(the_country(rank_up)),
    if (length(rank_up) == 1) " ranks" else " rank", " at least three places higher than by carbon."
  )
} else {
  ""
}
```

Over the full horizon the primary scenario clears `r fmt1(sum(rs_final$area_loss) / 1e6)` Mha more forest than BAU. `r sub("^the ", "The ", the_country(area_final$country[1]))`, `r the_country(area_final$country[2])` and `r the_country(area_final$country[3])` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(area_final$area_share[1:3]))`% of it. Area and carbon rank countries differently, because the extra forest cleared holds `r fmt0(sum(rs_final$carbon_loss) / sum(rs_final$area_loss))` t CO₂ per hectare on average, but `r fmt0(lowest_density$t_per_ha)` in `r the_country(lowest_density$country)` and `r fmt0(highest_density$t_per_ha)` in `r the_country(highest_density$country)`, the extremes among the ten countries that clear the most.`r rank_up_text` The country split has the same caveats as the carbon results ([Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix)).

### ILUC carbon intensity {#sec-results-iluc}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-iluc

iluc_central <- iluc[iluc$scenario == "vo_rs", ]
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Accounting period (years)" = iluc_central$years,
    "Additional loss (Gt CO₂)" = iluc_central$carbon_loss / 1e9,
    "ILUC (g CO₂/MJ)" = iluc_central$g_per_mj,
    "VO-RD total (g CO₂e/MJ)" = vord_direct_ci + iluc_central$g_per_mj,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = c(0, 2, 1, 1),
  caption = paste0(
    "ILUC carbon intensity of VO-RD in the primary scenario for each accounting period, using ",
    fmt1(vord_mj_2035 / 1e12), " EJ of VO-RD a year. VO-RD total adds the direct 42.3 g CO₂e/MJ ",
    "[@seber2025, p. 6]; the fossil baseline is 93.3 [@seber2025, p. 1]."
  )
)
```

Over the `r headline_years`-year headline period, ILUC is `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))` g CO₂/MJ. The 30-year value, `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 30))`, is the one to set against ICCT's 62 g CO₂e/MJ, which comes from a 2020–2050 window. Both benchmarks, ICCT's 62 and Chen et al.'s 84.1, are ILUC alone, so they compare with these values rather than with totals that include VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ. Ours count only forest biomass carbon, so they leave out the 47.5 g CO₂e/MJ Chen et al. add for peat and the 7.3 for non-peat soil. Their biomass carbon alone comes to `r chen_biomass_iluc`, before a credit of −29.4 for the carbon the new palms take up [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13].

```{r}
#| label: fig-iluc-by-country
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Each country's contribution to the primary scenario's ", headline_years, "-year ILUC value, split between the palm-only and soy-only runs.")

# Contributions to the headline ILUC estimate: each country's additional loss after
# headline_years years in the palm-only and soy-only runs, in g CO2 per MJ of VO-RD.
iluc_year <- min(lum$year) + headline_years
iluc_by_country <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(year == iluc_year, scenario %in% c("bau", "vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy")) |>
  dplyr::select(country, scenario, forest_carbon_tco2) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    palm = forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "bau"] - forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "vo_rs_palm"],
    soy = forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "bau"] - forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "vo_rs_soy"],
    .by = country
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(c(palm, soy), \(x) x * 1e6 / (headline_years * vord_mj_2035)),
    total = palm + soy
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(total))

iluc_top_n <- 10
iluc_top <- iluc_by_country$country[seq_len(iluc_top_n)]
iluc_other <- sprintf("Other %d countries", sum(iluc_by_country$total > 0) - iluc_top_n)
iluc_plot <- iluc_by_country |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = ifelse(country %in% iluc_top, country, iluc_other)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(`Oil palm` = sum(palm), Soybeans = sum(soy), .by = label)
iluc_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(label = iluc_plot$label, crop = "Oil palm", g_per_mj = iluc_plot$`Oil palm`),
  data.frame(label = iluc_plot$label, crop = "Soybeans", g_per_mj = iluc_plot$Soybeans)
)
iluc_plot$label <- factor(iluc_plot$label, levels = rev(c(iluc_top, iluc_other)))
iluc_totals <- iluc_plot |> dplyr::summarise(g_per_mj = sum(g_per_mj), .by = label)

ggplot2::ggplot(iluc_plot, ggplot2::aes(g_per_mj, label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(
    ggplot2::aes(fill = crop),
    position = ggplot2::position_stack(reverse = TRUE),
    width = 0.62, colour = col_surface, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = iluc_totals, ggplot2::aes(label = fmt1(g_per_mj)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_crop, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Contributions to the ILUC estimate by country and crop",
    subtitle = paste0("Primary scenario, ", headline_years, "-year accounting period"),
    x = expression("g CO"[2] * " per MJ of VO-RD"),
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Two countries, `r the_country(iluc_by_country$country[1])` and `r the_country(iluc_by_country$country[2])`, contribute `r fmt1(sum(iluc_by_country$total[1:2]))` of the `r fmt1(sum(iluc_by_country$total))` g CO₂/MJ, and the palm price increase accounts for `r fmt0(100 * sum(iluc_by_country$palm) / sum(iluc_by_country$total))`% of the total. Indonesia and Malaysia, the only countries Chen et al. study, contribute `r fmt1(im_iluc)`, against their `r chen_biomass_iluc` from biomass carbon.

### Sensitivity to the elasticities {#sec-results-sensitivity}

We repeat every step, from price shock to ILUC, with the two Roberts & Schlenker specifications that give the smallest and largest multiplier (@tbl-price-shock-check).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-iluc-sensitivity

# The primary scenario and the runs at the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates: their
# Table 1 specifications with the smallest and largest multiplier (setup chunk), each run through the
# model like the central case.
sens <- data.frame(
  case = c(
    paste0("Low end: smallest multiplier (", rs_low$spec, ")"), "Central values (primary scenario)",
    paste0("High end: largest multiplier (", rs_high$spec, ")")
  ),
  scenario = c("vo_rs_low", "vo_rs", "vo_rs_high"),
  eps_s = c(rs_low$eps_s, eps_s_rs, rs_high$eps_s),
  eps_d = c(rs_low$eps_d, eps_d_rs, rs_high$eps_d),
  shock = c(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low, shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs, shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high)
)
sens_il <- function(yrs) vapply(sens$scenario, il, numeric(1), yrs = yrs)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Roberts & Schlenker estimate" = sens$case,
    "Supply elasticity" = fmt_el(sens$eps_s),
    "Demand elasticity" = fmt_el(sens$eps_d),
    "Price shock, 2035" = paste0(fmt0(sens$shock), "%"),
    "ILUC, 20 years" = fmt1(sens_il(20)),
    "ILUC, 25 years" = fmt1(sens_il(25)),
    "ILUC, 30 years" = fmt1(sens_il(30)),
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = NULL
  ),
  align = "lrrrrrr",
  caption = paste(
    "ILUC carbon intensity of VO-RD (g CO₂/MJ) with Roberts & Schlenker's central values and at the low and",
    "high ends of their estimates: the two of their six Table 1 specifications with the smallest and largest",
    "multiplier [@roberts2013, p. 2279]. All three are run through the emLab model."
  )
)
```

Across Roberts & Schlenker's estimates, the `r headline_years`-year value runs from `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_low", 25))` to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_high", 25))` g CO₂/MJ, `r fmt0(100 * (1 - il("vo_rs_low", 25) / il("vo_rs", 25)))`% below and `r fmt0(100 * (il("vo_rs_high", 25) / il("vo_rs", 25) - 1))`% above the central value, roughly in step with the price shock (`r fmt0(100 * (1 - shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low / shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs))`% below and `r fmt0(100 * (shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high / shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs - 1))`% above). With VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ, the total runs from `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs_low", 25))` to `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs_high", 25))` g/MJ, against a fossil baseline of `r fossil_baseline_ci`. Over all three accounting periods the range is `r fmt1(min(iluc$g_per_mj))` to `r fmt1(max(iluc$g_per_mj))` g CO₂/MJ.

This range covers only the spread across Roberts & Schlenker's specifications. It leaves out the other uncertainties in [Caveats](#sec-caveats): the linear approximation, the use of staple-crop elasticities for vegetable oils, and the carbon pools we don't count.

## Caveats {#sec-caveats}

- The price shock comes from a linear approximation applied to a demand shift of `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of the market, so the true price response is probably larger. Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities are for staple calories (maize, wheat, rice and soybeans), not vegetable oils.
- The price shock takes its supply response from Roberts & Schlenker, which covers every source of extra supply: higher yields, other crops, and new farmland whether or not it was forest. The emLab model turns the price into forest clearing only, so we count no land-use change outside forests.
- Country results are the weakest part. One global price change applies everywhere, as if supply and the pass-through of world prices to farmers were the same in every country. Country effects are held at their 2016–2020 average, some small neighboring countries are pooled into regions, and each cell gets the crop mix of a broad GAEZ zone, which thins the palm response in the palm frontiers and spreads it into Central Africa ([Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix)). That probably explains why the Democratic Republic of the Congo ranks first.
- Only forest biomass carbon is counted, not peat, soil carbon or lost future sequestration. Peat alone was 614 of the 1,086 Tg CO₂e in Chen et al.'s estimate [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13], mostly in Indonesia and Malaysia. Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the model either. Both understate ILUC.
- The soybean price change uses an accounting share (0.353), not an estimated market response, and the oil-price shock makes no allowance for soy meal, which overstates it.
- Prices jump once and stay there, and cleared forest never grows back ([Methods](#sec-land-use-model)).

## Use of generative AI

We used Claude (Anthropic, model Opus 5.5) through Claude Code as a coding and writing assistant. It drafted and edited much of the R code, including the changes to the emLab model in [Appendix A](#sec-lum-changes), and much of this report's prose, and it helped find and check sources. GitHub Copilot's coding agent set up the initial Quarto report and GitHub Pages workflow. We set the research question and scenarios, chose the data sources and key assumptions, and reviewed the code and text. The AI tools are not authors, and we are responsible for all code, analysis and conclusions. The AI tools produced no data or results: every number, figure and table is computed by the code in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/emlab-ucsb/marine-biofuel-iluc-prototype) when the report is built.

## Appendix A: Changes to the emLab model code {#sec-lum-changes}

Every change we made to emLab's land-use model to run the price scenarios, for the model's authors to check. Starting point: upstream `emlab-ucsb/land-based-solutions`, `r/robert_test/parallelization/` at commit `e207c2b` (31 July 2026), copied to `r/land_use_model/` (see `r/land_use_model/PROVENANCE.md`). Anything not listed is unchanged.

**Unchanged:** `simulation_functions.R` (including `update_revenues()` and `simulate_10_dt()`), `packages.R`, `r/directories.R` (now only read from, via `paths.R`), the deforestation model and its coefficients, and the fixed-effect construction (pixel FEs, the 2016–2020 country-year FE window, asymmetric-information FEs).

**All scripts**

1. `r/robert_test/parallelization/` → `r/land_use_model/` in every `here::here()` path.

**New file: `paths.R`**

2. Defines the input root `input_wdir`, read via `r/directories.R` as `{data_directory}/parallelized` and treated as read-only, and the output root `wdir`, the repo's git-ignored `land_use_model_runs/`. It stops if `wdir` is inside any Nextcloud folder or inside the inputs. This is so our outputs can't sync over the shared Nextcloud files of the same name.

**`01_prepare_data.R`**

3. Carbon price fixed at 0: `CP_LIST` (10 carbon prices) replaced by `CP <- 0`.
4. New input `PRICE_SHOCKS` (Section 1): % price change per shocked crop, one element per scenario, with `bau` first and unshocked. Scenarios: `bau`; `vo_20pct` (smoke test, `Oil, palm` and `Soybeans` both +20%); `vo_rs`, built from the 2035 shock read from `data/derived/vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv` (`pct_delta_p_rs`, from Roberts & Schlenker's central supply and demand elasticities), with `Oil, palm` taking the full shock and `Soybeans` taking `SOY_OIL_VALUE_SHARE` (0.353, Janzen & Wang 2025) of it; `vo_rs_palm` and `vo_rs_soy`, the `vo_rs` shock applied to one crop at a time, for crop attribution; and `vo_rs_low` and `vo_rs_high`, the same mapping applied to the CSV's `pct_delta_p_rs_low` and `pct_delta_p_rs_high`, the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates, for a sensitivity analysis. The script stops if those two columns are missing. Sources for every number are in [Methods](#sec-mapping). (Earlier versions also ran `vo_central`, `vo_high` and `vo_rs_model`, with other elasticities; all three have been dropped.)
5. New Section 2b: expands `PRICE_SHOCKS` into `PRICE_SCENARIOS`, one full 17-crop price vector per scenario, starting from the `CPrice == 0` rows of `final_prices_allcp`. Writes `price_scenarios.csv`. Stops if a shocked crop isn't in the model, or if any crop in `endo_input_data` has no price.
6. Section 6: `update_revenues()` runs once per price scenario (`revenue_<scenario>` columns) instead of once per carbon price (`revenue_cp<P>`). BAU revenue is computed the same way instead of being taken from `data_past$revenue`, so every scenario uses one formula. The two BAU versions agree to ~1e-12, and the script prints that check on every run.
7. Section 8: chunk files carry `revenue_<scenario>` columns in place of `revenue_cp0` and `revenue_cp<P>`.
8. Section 8: the per-pixel attributes file `grid_smry.csv` also carries `lat` and `lon`, for mapping.
9. Section 11: `model_params.rds` stores `cp` and `price_scenarios` in place of `cp_list`.
10. Paths come from `paths.R` instead of the hard-coded `/Users/rheilmayr/Nextcloud/...` `wdir`, which upstream used for both inputs and outputs.

**`02_run_simulations.R`**

11. The 38 distinct simulations (56 labeled blocks across endog/exog, fi/fi_bl_vp/ai_bl_vp and carbon price) are replaced by one `simulate_10_dt()` run per price scenario, at `cp = 0` with `pixel_fe`. This is the same construction as upstream's `endog_fi_blvp` runs, $D(0, V(P))$, with scenario prices in place of carbon-price equilibrium prices.
12. Output parquet columns are `scn, pixel_id, year, biomass` (upstream: `crp_price, cprice, pixel_id, year, info, biomass`). The row-count check is now pixels × scenarios × years.
13. Paths come from `paths.R`, as in `01`.

**Disabled scripts**

14. `00_generate_sample_data.R`, `00c_run_cobweb.R`, `01b_prepare_uncertainty_draws.R`, `02b_run_simulations_uncertainty.R`, and `03_aggregate_results.R` through `09_conceptual_diagrams.R` (including `03b`) have a `stop()` as their first line. They still expect upstream's carbon-price outputs and use upstream's hard-coded paths, which on a colleague's machine point at the shared Nextcloud folder. `00` and `00c` write into `1_input/` itself. Each `stop()` comes out only when that script is adapted to `paths.R`.

**New file: `03_summarise_results.R`**

15. Reduces `02`'s per-pixel results to two files for the report, pairing each result file with its chunk file for each pixel's `country` and `CF`:
    - `data/derived/land_use_country_results.csv.gz`: country × scenario × year totals of forest carbon (`sum(biomass)`, t CO₂) and forest area (`sum(biomass / CF)`, ha, using upstream's `ha_per_pixel = CF_pix / CF`).
    - `data/derived/land_use_grid_loss.csv.gz`: per 0.5° grid square (from `grid_smry.csv` coordinates), 2020 forest carbon and final-year additional loss relative to BAU for each scenario, as carbon (t CO₂) and as forest area (ha, `biomass / CF`).

    Stops if BAU 2020 forest carbon doesn't match `01`'s `grid_smry.csv`, or if any scenario's gridded carbon or area loss doesn't sum to its country-level loss.

**`run_pipeline.R`**

16. `STAGES` runs `01` → `02` → `03_summarise_results.R`; upstream stages `03`–`07` are commented out.

Earlier versions of this list had items 17–19: a script that traced the model's own supply curves (`00d_supply_curve.R`), and per-pixel crop output in `01` and `03` for a check of how much oil the cleared land grows. We have dropped both analyses, deleted the script and reverted the code.

**Verification** (200-pixel sample inputs, `1_input/smpl`):

- BAU emissions per pixel, annualized the same way as `03`'s `bl_emit_co2_y`, match upstream's reference run (`5_validation/sim_results_exog_ref_smpl.csv`) to within 0.003% for all 201 pixels.
- `vo_20pct` biomass is never higher than BAU, and is lower in the 110 of 201 pixels that grow palm or soy.

**Verification** (full inputs, `1_input/full`, 1,450,769 pixels):

- BAU revenue recomputed with `update_revenues()` matches upstream's `data_past$revenue` to within 7e-12.
- At every pixel, biomass in 2035 and 2171 is never higher under a shock than under BAU.
- `vo_rs_low` and `vo_rs_high`: at every pixel, biomass in 2035 and 2171 is never higher under `vo_rs_high` than under `vo_rs`, nor under `vo_rs` than under `vo_rs_low`. Adding them left every country × year total of the existing scenarios unchanged.
- `vo_rs_palm` and `vo_rs_soy` sum to `vo_rs` to within 0.11% of its additional loss 15 years after the shock, and to within 0.02% at the end of the horizon.
- `03_summarise_results.R`: BAU 2020 forest carbon summed by country equals `01`'s per-pixel 2020 biomass, and each scenario's gridded carbon and area loss equal its country-level loss.
- Rerun on 3 November 2026 without `vo_rs_model` and with items 17–19 reverted: every country × scenario × year forest carbon and area total for the remaining seven scenarios (163,856 rows), and every gridded carbon loss, is identical to the previous run.
- Runtime on a 64 GB laptop, seven scenarios: `01` 266 s, `02` 160 s, `03_summarise_results.R` 48 s. Peak memory was ~31 GB in `01` when last measured, with eight scenarios.

## Appendix B: Results of the +20% test run {#sec-test-run}

The first run the model's authors asked for: palm and soybean prices both up 20% (soybeans by the full 20%, without the oil-share adjustment), at a zero carbon price and otherwise as in [Methods](#sec-land-use-model). It tests how the model responds; it is not a policy scenario.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-run-global

test_global <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("bau", "vo_20pct")) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    carbon = sum(forest_carbon_tco2),
    area = sum(forest_area_ha),
    .by = c(scenario, year)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(scenario, year)
test_bau <- test_global[test_global$scenario == "bau", ]
test_shock <- test_global[test_global$scenario == "vo_20pct", ]
stopifnot(identical(test_bau$year, test_shock$year))

base_year <- min(lum$year)
test_rows <- match(c(base_year + 1, 2035, 2050, final_year), test_bau$year)
bau_loss <- test_bau$carbon[test_bau$year == base_year] - test_bau$carbon[test_rows]
extra_loss <- test_bau$carbon[test_rows] - test_shock$carbon[test_rows]

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Years after shock" = test_bau$year[test_rows] - base_year,
    "BAU forest carbon loss (Gt CO₂)" = bau_loss / 1e9,
    "Additional loss, +20% (Gt CO₂)" = extra_loss / 1e9,
    "Additional loss, +20% (Mha)" = (test_bau$area[test_rows] - test_shock$area[test_rows]) / 1e6,
    "Additional as % of BAU loss (CO₂)" = 100 * extra_loss / bau_loss,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = c(0, 1, 3, 2, 2),
  caption = "+20% test run: cumulative forest carbon loss under BAU and additional loss from the price increase, all countries."
)
```

BAU loses `r fmt1(bau_loss[1] / 1e9)` Gt CO₂ of forest carbon in the first year, close to the ~4.2 Gt noted in a comment in upstream's `01_prepare_data.R` (Section 5). The 20% increase adds `r fmt1(100 * extra_loss[2] / bau_loss[2])`% to BAU's cumulative loss over 15 years. The share shrinks over longer horizons because BAU loss keeps accumulating while the extra loss levels off.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-run-countries

test_countries <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("bau", "vo_20pct"), year %in% c(2035, final_year)) |>
  dplyr::select(country, scenario, year, forest_carbon_tco2) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    extra_mt = (forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "bau"] - forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "vo_20pct"]) / 1e6,
    .by = c(country, year)
  )
test_top <- dplyr::inner_join(
  test_countries |> dplyr::filter(year == 2035) |> dplyr::select(country, extra_15 = extra_mt),
  test_countries |> dplyr::filter(year == final_year) |> dplyr::select(country, extra_full = extra_mt),
  by = "country"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share_pct = 100 * extra_full / sum(extra_full)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(extra_full)) |>
  utils::head(10)

knitr::kable(
  test_top,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Country", "Additional loss, 15 years (Mt CO₂)", "Additional loss, full horizon (Mt CO₂)", "Share of global (%)"),
  caption = "+20% test run: the ten countries with the largest additional forest carbon loss."
)
```

## Appendix C: Questions for the emLab model's authors {#sec-crop-mix}

This note is for the authors of emLab's land-use model. We want to confirm that we are using the model correctly, and we are not suggesting any change to it. The model was built for carbon prices, which compete with a cell's total agricultural revenue. We use it to shock just two crops, palm oil and soybeans, so how the model splits a cell's revenue among crops matters much more for us. Our four questions are [at the end](#sec-lum-questions).

```{r}
#| label: crop-mix-data

# Written by r/audit_crop_mix.R from the model's inputs (read-only) and this repository's model run.
cm_num <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "crop_mix_numbers.csv"))
cm <- function(metric) cm_num$value[cm_num$metric == metric]
cm_regions <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "crop_mix_regions.csv"))
cm_countries <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "crop_mix_countries.csv"))
cm_grid <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "crop_mix_grid.csv.gz"))
pct <- function(x) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = 1), "%")

# Share of the extra forest the primary scenario clears that the model counts as cropland
# (def_for_ag_share), weighted by area.
cropland <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "crop_mix_cropland_share.csv"))
cropland_pct <- function(scope, yrs) {
  100 * cropland$cropland_share[
    cropland$scope == scope & cropland$weight == "vo_rs extra clearing" & cropland$years %in% yrs
  ]
}
```

### The crop mix

- **The crop mix is set per zone.** Each cell's revenue (`update_revenues()`) and crop production (`endog_prices()`) weight crops by `harvested_share_gaez`. That share is the same for every cell with the same `gaez` value (`r fmt0(cm("gaez_zones"))` values, such as `54_Europe`). We assume this gives forest cells, which have little cropland of their own, the crop mix of the wider area.
- **For palm and soybeans, that mix differs a lot from the frontiers' own.** We look at four frontiers where palm or soybeans already make up much of the cropland: Riau, a province in central Sumatra, Indonesia, and Sabah and Sarawak, the Malaysian states on Borneo, for palm; and Mato Grosso, Brazil, and the Paraguayan Chaco for soybeans. For each crop's actual share of a cell's cropland we use the inputs' `m3_harvested_area_ha` column. We assume it comes from M3 [@monfreda2008], a global map of harvested area and yield for 175 crops around 2000, on a grid of about 10 km. In Riau, palm is `r pct(cm_regions$palm_share_m3[1])` of M3 harvested area but `r pct(cm_regions$palm_share_median[1])` of the model's crop mix, and no cell anywhere gets more than `r pct(cm("palm_share_max"))` (@tbl-crop-mix-frontiers). Palm is also more than 5% of the crop mix in `r fmt0(cm_countries$cells_palm_over_5pct[cm_countries$country == "Democratic Republic of the Congo"])` cells in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (@fig-crop-mix-map).
- **This shapes our country results.** A cell's revenue weights each crop's price by its share of the crop mix, so a palm price rise adds less revenue, and causes less clearing, where palm's share is small. As we use the model, the zone-level mix thins the palm response in the palm frontiers and spreads it into Central Africa. That probably explains why the Democratic Republic of the Congo has the most additional loss in our results.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-crop-mix-frontiers

frontier_crop <- c("Palm", "Palm", "Soybeans", "Soybeans")
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Frontier" = sub(" \\(.*", "", cm_regions$region),
    "Crop" = frontier_crop,
    "Share of crop mix, model" = pct(ifelse(frontier_crop == "Palm", cm_regions$palm_share_median, cm_regions$soy_share_median)),
    "Share of harvested area, M3" = pct(ifelse(frontier_crop == "Palm", cm_regions$palm_share_m3, cm_regions$soy_share_m3)),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "llrr",
  caption = paste(
    "The frontier crop's share in four frontiers. Model: harvested_share_gaez (median cell).",
    "M3: the crop's share of all 17 crops' M3 harvested area (m3_harvested_area_ha) in the same cells."
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-crop-mix-map
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8.6
#| fig-cap: "Palm's share of the crop mix in each 0.5° square: as the model uses it (harvested_share_gaez, averaged over the square's cells), and from M3 harvested area in the same cells."

share_classes <- c("0", "< 1%", "1–5%", "5–10%", "10–20%", "20–50%", "≥ 50%", "No M3 cropland")
share_class <- function(x) {
  cls <- as.character(cut(x, c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = share_classes[2:7]))
  factor(ifelse(is.na(x), "No M3 cropland", ifelse(x == 0, "0", cls)), levels = share_classes)
}
map_panels <- c(model = "Crop mix the model uses (harvested_share_gaez, set per GAEZ zone)", m3 = "M3 harvested area in the same cells")
palm_map <- rbind(
  data.frame(lon = cm_grid$lon, lat = cm_grid$lat, panel = map_panels[["model"]], class = share_class(cm_grid$palm_share_model)),
  data.frame(lon = cm_grid$lon, lat = cm_grid$lat, panel = map_panels[["m3"]], class = share_class(cm_grid$palm_share_m3))
)
palm_map$panel <- factor(palm_map$panel, levels = map_panels)

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_polygon(
    data = basemap,
    ggplot2::aes(lon, lat, group = piece, subgroup = ring),
    fill = col_land, colour = col_surface, linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(data = palm_map, ggplot2::aes(lon, lat, fill = class), width = 0.5, height = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
    values = stats::setNames(c("#e6e4dc", map_ramp(6), "#a9a79f"), share_classes),
    breaks = share_classes,
    name = "Palm share of the crop mix",
    drop = FALSE,
    guide = ggplot2::guide_legend(nrow = 1, title.position = "top", label.position = "bottom", keywidth = ggplot2::unit(1.6, "cm"), keyheight = ggplot2::unit(0.3, "cm"))
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(-57, 84), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_map() +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", hjust = 0))
```

### Reading the results

We count all the extra forest the model clears as ILUC, whatever the land is used for afterwards. The model itself counts only part of it as cropland: in each cell, the share of its 2000–2020 forest loss that became cropland or palm (`def_for_ag_share`). Weighted by area, that is `r fmt0(cropland_pct("All countries", 1))`% of the extra forest the primary scenario clears in its first year and `r fmt0(cropland_pct("All countries", 25))`% after 25 years: `r fmt0(cropland_pct("Indonesia", 25))`% in Indonesia and `r fmt0(cropland_pct("Malaysia", 25))`% in Malaysia, but `r fmt1(cropland_pct("Democratic Republic of the Congo", 25))`% in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The primary shock also puts palm at `r fmt1(1 + shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs / 100)` times its 2020 price. Over the range of our sensitivity runs the model's response is close to proportional: from the low end to the high end, the price shock rises `r fmt0(100 * (shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high / shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low - 1))`% and the `r headline_years`-year carbon loss `r fmt0(100 * (il("vo_rs_high", headline_years) / il("vo_rs_low", headline_years) - 1))`% ([Sensitivity](#sec-results-sensitivity)).

Until we hear back, we caution against reading our country results as a map of where palm-driven deforestation would happen.

### Our questions {#sec-lum-questions}

On the crop mix:

1. Is a price change for individual crops, like ours, a use of the model you would expect to work, given that the crop mix is set per GAEZ zone?
2. Given the crop mix, would you report our results by country, or only as global totals?

On reading the results:

3. Is it right to count all the extra forest the model clears as ILUC, even though the model counts only `r fmt0(cropland_pct("All countries", 25))`% of it as cropland after 25 years?
4. Are you comfortable using the model's response at palm prices `r fmt1(1 + shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs / 100)` times the 2020 level?

`r/audit_crop_mix.R` reproduces every number here from the unmodified inputs and this repository's model run.
